Good morning! I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a quick tool called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—which asks about mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past week. It’s completely confidential; your answers help us figure out the best support for you right now. There are ten short questions, and I’ll ask them in everyday language so you can just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say always, most of the time, sometimes, or hardly ever?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast*

Hardly ever... I mean, I try when my husband makes jokes, but it's like I have to force it. Nothing really feels funny anymore. I used to laugh all the time before the baby came.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Hardly ever… I hear my husband trying to joke and I make myself smile, but it feels fake. I just don’t feel that laughter inside anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it’s like, why bother? Everything feels flat. I still do them sometimes, but I don’t *look forward* to anything the way I used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Even when my husband says he’s just being a normal newborn, I keep replaying everything in my head and feeling like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most of the time… I know some worry is normal, but even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing, he’s fed, he’s sleeping—I still feel this knot in my chest, convinced something bad is about to happen. I check the monitor every few minutes and still lie awake waiting for something to go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… it’s like a sudden wave. I’ll be folding the baby’s clothes and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days I feel like I’m drowning in little tasks. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep, washing bottles—on paper it looks simple, but it piles up and I end up sitting on the couch crying because I can’t see how to get through the next hour, let alone the rest of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… even when the baby finally settles, I lie there staring at the ceiling with my mind racing—going over everything I think I did wrong, worrying something will happen to him, feeling like I’m failing. Some nights I fall asleep for an hour and then jolt awake and can’t get back to sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time… I wake up already feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Little things make me tear up—seeing the sunrise, hearing a lullaby, even when the baby smiles. I keep thinking I should feel happy, but mostly I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… pretty much every day this week. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I’m rocking him, sometimes it’s full-on sobbing when my partner takes the baby so I can shower. I feel like I’m crying over nothing and everything all at once.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has been replaced by a heavy, gray cloud that hangs over each day. Despite your love for your baby, you feel constantly overwhelmed, tearful, and unable to enjoy even simple pleasures. You blame yourself whenever your son fusses, lie awake racked with worry, and experience sudden surges of panic that leave you shaky. You cry daily and feel as though you're failing at motherhood, yet you clearly want to be the best mom you can be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter and finds attempts forced and inauthentic, mapping to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure ("flat," "why bother?") matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') and gives vivid examples of blaming herself for normal infant behavior, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, disproportionate worry "most of the time" despite objective safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes that occur "sometimes," matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being overwhelmed "most days," feeling unable to manage basic tasks to the point of crying and not knowing how to proceed, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, severe sleep disruption most nights, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness and tearfulness "most of the time," matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS guidelines indicate scores ≥14 (or any positive response on Item 10) warrant urgent assessment. This patient scored 26/30, endorsing severe symptoms across all mood/anxiety domains: marked <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1, Q2), excessive <sym>self-blame</sym> (Q3), persistent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> (Q4, Q5), overwhelming inability to cope (Q6), <sym>insomnia</sym> driven by rumination (Q7), and near-constant <sym>low mood</sym> with daily crying (Q8, Q9). These findings meet DSM-5 threshold for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. No suicidal ideation was reported (Q10 score 0), so immediate safety concern is reduced, yet functional impairment is high. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Begin evidence-based treatment (consider <med>CBT</med> and/or <med>sertraline</med> if breastfeeding-compatible)
3. Coordinate practical support: partner/family help with night feeds, meal delivery, housework
4. Introduce 15-minute daily solo breaks; schedule pleasurable micro-activities
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing at first sign of <sym>panic surge</sym>; limit monitor checks to once per hour after midnight
6. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks to track response
7. Provide 24-hour crisis line number for reassurance and safety backup
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: **Postpartum Depression Screening Summary**

**Symptoms & Observations**  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, absent anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood described as “empty,” “gray,” “weepy”; daily crying spells  
- Pronounced guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Chronic, intrusive anxiety and episodic panic (physical symptoms, catastrophic expectations)  
- Sleep disruption driven by rumination and hypervigilance toward infant  
- Frequent feeling of being overwhelmed by routine tasks  

**Pattern**  
Consistent dysphoric–anxious presentation across all domains; symptoms present “most of the time” and functionally impairing.  

**Screening Significance**  
Responses align with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; no current self-harm ideation reported.  

**Risk Factors Noted**  
- Daily crying, anhedonia, guilt, sleep–mood linkage → elevated PPD risk  
- Panic-equivalent episodes → possible postpartum anxiety disorder  
- Absence of suicidal thoughts; safety concern currently negative.
